## Friday's Question

Is the converse true? Is every perfect square a glow number?

::: notes
Yes. A perfect square is m^2 for a positive integer m, and
m^2 = T_{m-1} + T_m, so the witness is k = m.

Both definitions are for positive integers, so 0 never comes up, and T_0 = 0
is defined, so 1 = T_0 + T_1 is a glow number.

The theorem and its converse together: the glow numbers are exactly the
perfect squares. Proving the converse means naming a k for a given m -- an
existential, proved by giving the witness.
:::

## Today’s goals

- Understand role of components of an inductive proof.
- Write short inductive proofs.


## Warm Up {.activity}

A *Tower* is built by stacking 5m red panels, and 7m blue panels.

What tower heights are possible? Talk it through with the people around you:
which heights can you build, and which can't you?

{{< countdown minutes=10 >}}

::: notes
Give this time -- it took a while last year. Let them find the last height
that cannot be built (23) themselves.

End up with a clear claim: For all n > 23, we can build a tower of
height n using only 5m red and 7m blue panels.

Say "claim holds for smaller values"
:::

## Warm Up Continued {.smaller}

Claim: for all integers $n > 23$, we can build a tower of height
$n$ using only 5m red and 7m blue panels.

::: {.fillable}
| Height | Red | Blue |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 24 | | |
| 25 | | |
| 26 | | |
| 27 | | |
| 28 | | |
: {tbl-colwidths="[30,35,35]"}
:::

Every height $n \geq 29$: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
24 = 2 red + 2 blue. 25 = 5 red. 26 = 1 red + 3 blue. 27 = 4 red + 1 blue.
28 = 4 blue.

Every n >= 29: n - 5 is at least 24, so a tower of height n - 5 can be built.
Add one red panel.

Why FIVE base cases: each height comes from the height 5 below it, so the
first five have to be checked by hand. Three is not enough -- 28 would need
23, which cannot be built. (27 would need 22, which can be built, but the claim
says nothing about 22.) Worth asking before filling in the table.

Point out the universal quantifier, and the least value. This is proof by
cases plus one new move: assume it for a smaller value (n - 5). That is
induction, before it has a name.

Aside, only if it comes up: 23 = 5*7 - 5 - 7.
:::

## Inductive Proof Skeleton Card


<div class="card">

Proof by Induction of $\forall n, P(n)$

1. First line: "Consider an arbitrary n." 
2. Second line (IH): "Assume $\forall j < n, P(j)$."
3. Determine exhaustive cases for $n$, including one or more base cases and usually one inductive case.
4. Prove each case, base and inductive, independently. Base case is typically direct, and inductive case will require use of IH.

</div>

::: {.fillable}
| | Claim | The smaller pieces |
|---|---|---|
| HW1 | every WFF has atoms = binary connectives + 1 | |
| HW2 | every expression has a CNF | |
| Today | every height $n > 23$ can be built | |
: {tbl-colwidths="[12,58,30]"}
:::

Check the smallest cases. Assume the claim for the smaller pieces. Show it
for the whole.

::: notes
HW1: the WFFs a formula is built from. HW2: the two expressions joined by an
and or an or. Today: the tower of height n - 5.

The name is structural induction when the smaller pieces are parts of the
thing; induction on n when they are smaller integers. Same skeleton. HW2
promised "we will study it formally in a few weeks" -- this is that.
:::

## Proof by Induction {.smaller}

Claim: For any integer $n > 0$, $\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n} k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$.

\

Proof: Consider an arbitrary integer $n > 0$. 

\

IH: Assume inductively that for any $j<n$, $\sum\limits_{k=1}^{j} k^2 = \frac{j(j+1)(2j+1)}{6}$.

\
